query: Context: we are writing our own physics-based (first-principles, no parameters fitted to keyhole data) model of laser keyholing and keyhole-mode melt-pool size for laser powder bed fusion of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend, to replace the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing Module where conduction models (Eagar-Tsai) fail. Settings: 1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam with 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s, 30-150 C plate. The model has three parts: (1) absorptivity from the Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid metal with multiple reflections ray-traced inside the keyhole; (2) the keyhole's depth and shape from an energy balance at a wall held near the boiling point (moving line/point sources, Kaplan-style local conduction, evaporation losses, recoil pressure against surface tension); (3) the melt pool as the liquidus isotherm of the resulting sources. We will check it against Gan et al. 2021 (Nat. Commun. 12, 2379) X-ray keyhole depths for Ti-6Al-4V, Al6061 and SS316, and against the AM Module's maps. Question: which physics-based reduced-order keyhole models predict keyhole depth and shape without fitting to keyhole data, and how well? Cover: Kaplan's point-by-point energy balance at the keyhole wall (J. Phys. D 1994) and his later Fresnel-absorption analysis; the conical keyhole of Lankalapalli, Tu and Gartner (J. Phys. D 1996); the front-wall drilling model of Fabbro and Chouf (J. Appl. Phys. 2000) and Fabbro's later scaling of keyhole depth; the point-plus-line source of Steen, Dowden and Davis (1988); the recoil-pressure energy balance of Semak and Matsunawa (1997); recoil pressure as about 0.54 of the saturated vapour pressure and the 18 % back-flux (Anisimov 1968; Knight 1979); multiple-reflection absorptivity of a cavity (Gouffe; ray tracing). For each give the governing equations with their symbols, the assumptions (wall temperature, cross-section shape, latent heat, evaporation), and any quantitative comparison with measured keyhole depths, especially in-situ X-ray depths in LPBF (Cunningham 2019, Gan 2021, Simonds 2021) and for aluminium alloys. Which assumption most limits accuracy at LPBF scales (beam radius 40-70 um, 0.3-1.5 m/s)? Give DOIs.
task_summary: Review Physics Based Reduced Order Keyhole Models Predicting Depth Shape Equations Assumptions Comparisons DOIs

info.name: update_plan

replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child

        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting

        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing

        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_plan

Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective

    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,

    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

Relevant Snippet:
A model describing the process of deep-penetration laser welding has been developed by calculating the keyhole profile using a point-by-point determination of the energy balance at the keyhole wall. A formula for heat conduction was derived from the model of a moving line source of heat. The various absorption mechanisms were modelled. The corresponding absorbed power transferred to the keyhole wall balances the conduction losses, which yields the local inclination of the wall. The thermodynamics and the flow of metal vapour inside the keyhole have been calculated. Accordingly, beam damping due to the plasma plume above the workpiece and the mean plasma absorption coefficient in the keyhole could be estimated. The keyhole profile tends to a geometry that distributes the major part of the beam to the front wall owing to higher conduction losses at the upstream side. The reasons for decreasing energy absorption with increasing welding speed are discussed.

Laser welding of aluminium alloys is an important industrial technology and yet many challenges still lie ahead. Laser welding studies were reported almost within two years since the first laser was invented in 1960. However, practical metal seam welding was not feasible until the early 1970s when multi-kilowatt, continuous wave CO2 lasers were developed to allow for deep penetration keyhole welding (Duley, 1999). Unfortunately, the application for deep penetration welding of aluminium was limited due to its very high reflectivity at the relatively long wavelength (10.6 micron) of CO2 lasers. Flash-pumped Nd:YAG lasers with a 1.06 micron wavelength were not suitable due to their low power and extremely poor efficiency at the time. Since the 1980s, high power seam welding of carbon steels using multi-kilowatt CO2 lasers has become a regular industrial practice, in particular in the automotive industry. In the mid 1990s, diode pumped Nd:YAG lasers were developed that offered kilowatt power and high efficiency. As a result, aluminium laser welding became more feasible because the beam absorption of aluminium alloys at 1.06 micron is three times as much as it is at 10.6 micron. Nevertheless, the poor beam quality and high cost of diodepumped Nd:YAG lasers still hinders their acceptance in industry. In the early 2000s, with the arrival of single-mode and multi-mode high power fiber lasers at a 1.075 micron wavelength, along with excellent beam quality and low maintenance cost, the expectation was that the advantage of laser welding aluminium components could be better realized. The requirement of very high laser power for aluminium welding is not only due to its high reflectivity and high heat conductivity. Aluminium has been known to be one of the most challenging metals to weld successfully (Mandal, 2002). Abstract:
Depending of the laser operating parameters, several characteristic regimes of laser welding can be observed. At low welding speeds, the aspect ratio of the keyhole can be rather large with a rather vertical cylindrical shape, whereas at high welding speeds, low aspect ratios result, where only the keyhole front is mainly irradiated. For these different regimes, the dependence of the keyhole (KH) depth or the keyhole threshold, as a function of the operating parameters and material properties, is derived and their resulting scaling laws are surprisingly very similar. This approach allows us to analyze the keyhole behavior for these welding regimes, around their keyhole generation thresholds. Specific experiments confirm the occurrence and the behavior of these unstable keyholes for these conditions. Furthermore, recent experimental results can be analyzed using these approaches. Finally, this analysis allows us to define the aspect ratio range for the occurrence of this unstable behavior and to highlight the importance of laser absorptivity for this mechanism. Consequently, the use of a short wavelength laser for the reduction of these keyhole stability issues and the corresponding improvement of weld seam quality is emphasized.

Abstract:
The key to keyhole formation The formation of keyholes, or vapor-filled depressions, during laser welding presents a large problem for additive manufacturing. Cunningham et al. used high-speed x-ray imaging to take a detailed look at keyhole formation in a titanium alloy. They found a simplified relationship between operational parameters and keyhole shape, which may allow for the prevention of pore formation going forward. Science, this issue p. 849 Keyhole formation and morphology in a titanium alloy depend on laser power and scanning speed. We used ultrahigh-speed synchrotron x-ray imaging to quantify the phenomenon of vapor depressions (also known as keyholes) during laser melting of metals as practiced in additive manufacturing. Although expected from welding and inferred from postmortem cross sections of fusion zones, the direct visualization of the keyhole morphology and dynamics with high-energy x-rays shows that (i) keyholes are present across the range of power and scanning velocity used in laser powder bed fusion; (ii) there is a well-defined threshold from conduction mode to keyhole based on laser power density; and (iii) the transition follows the sequence of vaporization, depression of the liquid surface, instability, and then deep keyhole formation. These and other aspects provide a physical basis for three-dimensional printing in laser powder bed machines.

Relevant Snippet:
The keyhole formed during penetration welding with a laser is modelled so far as its thermal absorption characteristics are concerned by the combination of a point and a line source. In this way a representation of the broader surface section of the weld is obtained in addition to the lower section. A simple analytical form for the temperature distribution is obtained and possible weld profiles are found numerically from this. These are compared with examples of actual welds; it is possible in this way to estimate the proportion of the laser power absorbed in each section of the weld. Graphs and some simple approximations are given which allow it to be done easily for a given weld.

Abstract:
The complexity of the phenomena simultaneously occurring, from the very first instants of high-power laser pulse interaction with the target up to the phase explosion, along with the strong changes in chemical-physical properties of matter, makes modeling laser ablation a hard task, especially near the thermodynamic critical regime. In this work, we report a computational model of an aluminum target irradiated in vacuum by a gaussian-shaped pulse of 20 ns duration, with a peak intensity of the order of GW/cm2. This continuum model covers laser energy deposition and temperature evolution in the irradiated target, along with the mass removal mechanism involved, and the vaporized material expansion. Aluminum was considered to be a case study due to the vast literature on the temperature dependence of its thermodynamic, optical, and transport properties that were used to estimate time-dependent values of surface-vapor quantities (vapor pressure, vapor density, vapor and surface temperature) and vapor gas-dynamical quantities (density, velocity, pressure) as it expands into vacuum. Very favorable agreement is reported with experimental data regarding: mass removal and crater depth due to vaporization, generated recoil momentum, and vapor flow velocity expansion.

Abstract:
Different processes require the detachment of metal drops from a solid material using a laser beam as the heat source, for instance laser drop generation or cyclam. These techniques imply that the drops enter the laser beam, which might affect their trajectory. Also, many laser processes such as laser welding or additive manufacturing generate spatters that can be accelerated by the laser beam during flight and create defects on the material. This fundamental study aims at investigating the effects of a continuous power laser beam on the acceleration of intentionally detached drops and unintentionally detached spatters. Two materials were studied: 316L steel and AlSi5 aluminium alloy. High-speed imaging was used to measure the position of the drops and calculate their acceleration to compare it to theoretical models. Accelerations up to 11.2 g could be measured. The contributions of the vapor pressure, the recoil pressure, and the radiation pressure were investigated. The recoil pressure was found to be the main driving effect but other phenomena counteract this acceleration and reduce it by an order of magnitude of one to two. In addition, two different vaporization regimes were observed, resulting respectively in a vapor plume and in a vapor halo around the drop.

Abstract:
Although metal vaporisation has been observed in several laser processes such as drilling or welding, vapour plume expansion and its induced side effects are not fully understood. Especially, this phenomenon is garnering scientific and industrial interest since recent investigations in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) have designated metal vaporisation as main source of denudation and powder spattering. The present study aims to provide a new insight on the dynamics of laser-induced vaporisation and to assess the potential of different gases for particle entrainment. A self-consistent finite element model of laser-induced keyhole and plume is thus presented for this purpose, built from a comprehensive literature review. The model is validated with dedicated experimental diagnostics, involving high-speed imaging to measure the ascent velocity of the vapour plume. The transient dynamics of vapour plume is thus quantified for different laser incident intensities and gas flow patterns such as the mushroom-like structure of the vapour plume are analysed. Finally, the model is used as a tool to quantify the entrainment flow expected in LPBF and an analytical model is derived to define a velocity threshold for particle entrainment, expressed in term of background gas properties. Doing so it is possible to predict how denudation evolves when the gaseous atmosphere is changed.

Abstract:
Metal three-dimensional (3D) printing includes a vast number of operation and material parameters with complex dependencies, which significantly complicates process optimization, materials development, and real-time monitoring and control. We leverage ultrahigh-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging and high-fidelity multiphysics modeling to identify simple yet universal scaling laws for keyhole stability and porosity in metal 3D printing. The laws apply broadly and remain accurate for different materials, processing conditions, and printing machines. We define a dimensionless number, the Keyhole number, to predict aspect ratio of a keyhole and the morphological transition from stable at low Keyhole number to chaotic at high Keyhole number. Furthermore, we discover inherent correlation between keyhole stability and porosity formation in metal 3D printing. By reducing the dimensions of the formulation of these challenging problems, the compact scaling laws will aid process optimization and defect elimination during metal 3D printing, and potentially lead to a quantitative predictive framework. Identifying scaling laws in metal 3D printing is key to process optimization and materials development. Here the authors report scaling laws to quantify correlation between process parameters, keyhole stability and pore formation by high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging and multiphysics modeling.

Abstract:
Keyhole porosity is a key concern in laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF), potentially impacting component fatigue life. However, some keyhole porosity formation mechanisms, e.g., keyhole fluctuation, collapse and bubble growth and shrinkage, remain unclear. Using synchrotron X-ray imaging we reveal keyhole and bubble behaviour, quantifying their formation dynamics. The findings support the hypotheses that: (i) keyhole porosity can initiate not only in unstable, but also in the transition keyhole regimes created by high laser power-velocity conditions, causing fast radial keyhole fluctuations (2.5–10 kHz); (ii) transition regime collapse tends to occur part way up the rear-wall; and (iii) immediately after keyhole collapse, bubbles undergo rapid growth due to pressure equilibration, then shrink due to metal-vapour condensation. Concurrent with condensation, hydrogen diffusion into the bubble slows the shrinkage and stabilises the bubble size. The keyhole fluctuation and bubble evolution mechanisms revealed here may guide the development of control systems for minimising porosity. Understanding the keyhole porosity formation is important in laser powder bed fusion. Here the authors reveal the dynamics of keyhole fluctuation, and collapse that induces bubble formation with three main stages of evolution; growth, shrinkage, and being captured by the solidification front.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Metal additive manufacturing (AM) offers unprecedented opportunities to fabricate complex, lightweight metallic components, yet its practical deployment remains fundamentally constrained by defects arising from rapid melting and solidification. Cyclic thermal transients generate cracks, pores, residual stresses, and lack-of-fusion regions, undermining mechanical performance and reliability. Ultrasonic field-assisted laser-based additive manufacturing (UF-LBAM) has emerged as a powerful approach to manipulate melt pool dynamics and suppress defect formation. Nevertheless, the governing physical mechanisms remain poorly understood, particularly under highly non-equilibrium ultrasonic excitation, where acoustic pressure oscillations, melt convection, cavitation, and solidification are intricately coupled across multiple temporal and spatial scales. Here, we provide a systematic review of X-ray based fundamental studies in UF-LBAM and the diverse applications of machine learning (ML), detailing the literature selection criteria and methodology. We highlight advances spanning synchrotron X-ray revealed physical phenomena, ML-driven real-time monitoring and defect prediction, and pathways toward industrial implementation. Critical challenges persist, including fundamental physics gaps, transferability of ML models across alloy systems, and real-time control limitations. We further identify promising directions for the field, such as physics-informed models, multimodal diagnostics, and closed-loop control, which together promise to unlock the full potential of UF-LBAM for high-performance metal component fabrication.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The metal additive manufacturing industry is actively developing instruments and strategies to enable higher productivity, optimal build quality, and controllable as-built microstructure. A beam controlling technique, laser oscillation has shown potential in all these aspects in laser welding; however, few attempts have been made to understand the underlying physics of the oscillating keyholes/melt pools which are the prerequisites for these strategies to become a useful tool for laser-based additive manufacturing processes. Here, to address this gap, we utilized a synchrotron-based X-ray operando technique to image the dynamic keyhole oscillation in Ti-6Al-4V using a miniature powder bed fusion setup. We found good agreement between the experimental observations and simulations performed with a validated Lattice Boltzmann multiphysics model. The study revealed the continuous and periodic fluctuations in the characteristic keyhole parameters that are unique to the oscillating laser beam processing and responsible for the chevron pattern formation at solidification. In particular, despite the intrinsic longer-range fluctuation, the oscillating technique displayed potential for reducing keyhole instability, mitigating porosity formation, and altering surface topology. These insights on the oscillating keyhole dynamics can be useful for the future development and application of this technique. Beam oscillation is an attractive method to achieve melt pool and microstructure control in laser powder bed additive manufacturing. Here, in-situ X-ray imaging and high-fidelity modeling reveal the unique keyhole dynamics in a kHz laser oscillation mode.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is a metal additive manufacturing technique involving complex interplays between vapor, liquid, and solid phases. Despite LPBF’s advantageous capabilities compared to conventional manufacturing methods, the underlying physical phenomena can result in inter-regime instabilities followed by transitions between conduction and keyhole melting regimes — leading to defects. We investigate these issues through operando synchrotron X-ray imaging synchronized with acoustic emission recording, during the remelting processes of LPBF-produced thin walls, monitoring regime changes occurring under constant laser processing parameters. As a result, conduction, stable keyhole, and unstable keyhole regimes are identified with a time resolution of 100 µs, even under rapid transitions, providing a straightforward method to accurately detect undesired processing regimes without the use of artificial intelligence.

Abstract:
Porosity in directed energy deposition (DED) deteriorates mechanical performances of components, limiting safety-critical applications. However, how pores arise and evolve in DED remains unclear. Here, we reveal pore evolution mechanisms during DED using in situ X-ray imaging and multi-physics modelling. We quantify five mechanisms contributing to pore formation, migration, pushing, growth, removal and entrapment: (i) bubbles from gas atomised powder enter the melt pool, and then migrate circularly or laterally; (ii) small bubbles can escape from the pool surface, or coalesce into larger bubbles, or be entrapped by solidification fronts; (iii) larger coalesced bubbles can remain in the pool for long periods, pushed by the solid/liquid interface; (iv) Marangoni surface shear flow overcomes buoyancy, keeping larger bubbles from popping out; and (v) once large bubbles reach critical sizes they escape from the pool surface or are trapped in DED tracks. These mechanisms can guide the development of pore minimisation strategies.

Abstract:
Keyhole instability during laser welding and laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) can cause keyhole collapse and pore formation. Using high-speed x-ray imaging, we demonstrate that the flow vortex-induced protrusion on the rear keyhole wall is crucial in initiating keyhole instability. Applying a transverse magnetic field suppresses the keyhole instability by driving a secondary thermoelectric magnetohydrodynamics (TEMHD) flow that alters the net flow vortex. This minimizes protrusions and large-amplitude keyhole oscillations. The suppression effectiveness depends on the laser scanning direction relative to the magnetic field orientation because this controls the Seebeck effect-induced Lorentz force's direction. We show that at LPBF length scales, electromagnetic damping is weak, and for alloys with a large Seebeck coefficient, TEMHD becomes the dominant mechanism controlling flow behind the keyhole.

Abstract:
Ultrasonic processing of solidifying metals in additive manufacturing can provide grain refinement and advantageous mechanical properties. However, the specific physical mechanisms of microstructural refinement relevant to laser-based additive manufacturing have not been directly observed because of sub-millimeter length scales and rapid solidification rates associated with melt pools. Here, high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging is used to observe the effect of ultrasonic vibration directly on melt pool dynamics and solidification of Al6061 alloy. The high temporal and spatial resolution enabled direct observation of cavitation effects driven by a 20.2 kHz ultrasonic source. We utilized multiphysics simulations to validate the postulated connection between ultrasonic treatment and solidification. The X-ray results show a decrease in melt pool and keyhole depth fluctuations during melting and promotion of pore migration toward the melt pool surface with applied sonication. Additionally, the simulation results reveal increased localized melt pool flow velocity, cooling rates, and thermal gradients with applied sonication. This work shows how ultrasonic treatment can impact melt pools and its potential for improving part quality.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion is a promising technology for local deposition and microstructure control, but it suffers from defects such as delamination and porosity due to the lack of understanding of melt pool dynamics. To study the fundamental behavior of the melt pool, both geometric and thermal sensing with high spatial and temporal resolutions are necessary. This work applies and integrates three advanced sensing technologies: synchrotron X-ray imaging, high-speed IR camera, and high-spatial-resolution IR camera to characterize the evolution of the melt pool shape, keyhole, vapor plume, and thermal evolution in Ti–6Al–4V and 410 stainless steel spot melt cases. Quantifications on boundary velocities, melt pool dimensions, thermal gradients, and cooling rates are performed, enabling future comprehensive melt pool dynamics and microstructure analysis. The study discovers a strong correlation between the thermal and X-ray data, demonstrating the feasibility of using relatively cheap IR cameras to predict features that currently can only be captured using costly synchrotron X-ray imaging. Such correlation can be used for future thermal-based melt pool control and model validation.

Abstract:
The laser-material interaction Katrin Wudy for laser-material processes, such as laser welding, where several phase changes occur, still needs to be fully understood. The high energy input in the material in a short time and small space renders the laser-material interaction a complex and highly dynamic mechanism. This interaction and the resulting radiation absorption govern the process behavior during manufacturing and, in turn, the quality of parts. In situ monitoring of the laser radiation absorption can be facilitated to evaluate the process. The absorption can be determined using an integrating sphere. To employ such a measuring system reliably without intense calibration effort for high throughput experiments, the robustness of the measuring signal toward changes to the system is crucial. This work evaluates said robustness by a series of experiments for which the signal of the integrating sphere diode and the back-reflection sensor of the laser are considered. The measuring system was altered by varying the electronic gain and the distance between the sphere and the specimen. Multiple experiments with varying laser powers were conducted for every configuration of the measuring system. Additionally, the stability of the reflective properties of the coated inner sphere was evaluated by analyzing the change in the measurements over time. The experimental results show the robustness of the integrating sphere signal trend toward the changes in the measurement parameters and degradation of the inner sphere coating. These are properties of a robust measuring system, which has excellent use in high throughput experiments for fundamental research in laser-material interaction.

Abstract:
Laser melting can be conducted in two different process regimes, the conduction and the keyhole mode, which exhibit significantly different characteristics, dynamics, and stability and are highly sensitive to a magnitude of process parameters. Despite these differences and the resulting high relevance of the prevailing process regime for process development, the regime is commonly deduced after specimen testing. An identification of the regime parallel to the process could speed up the process development of, for example, laser beam welding or laser-based powder bed fusion of metals. Therefore, the possibility of an in situ regime identification under process-near conditions is the aim of these investigations. For this, the absorbance is measured in situ by using an integrating sphere on an in-house-developed test rig. This test rig can mimic real production process conditions to detect the characteristic change in the degree of absorption when switching between the process regimes. These measurements were conducted during experiments in which only the laser power was varied. A significant change in absorption was detected at a threshold laser power of 100 W, which correlates with the transition between the process regimes’ conduction and keyhole regime. This threshold was proven by subsequent identification analysis of micrographic cross sections. This correlation promises the possibility of fast in situ process regime identification under near-real production process conditions with the potential of accelerating process development.

In this paper, a numerical simulation of the LBW process, considering the 3D transient heat transfer, fluid flow, and keyhole dynamics, is implemented, in which the free surface is tracked by the volume-of-fluid algorithm. The occurrence and evolution of porosity and the occasional blowout of melt need to be understood. Here, a recently developed X‐ray tomoscopy setup is applied, providing one hundred 3D images per second to capture the temporal evolution of the melt pool in an AlSi9Cu3(Fe) die‐casting while a laser beam advances. Abstract:
Laser-beam absorptance in a keyhole is generally calculated using either a ray-tracing method or electrodynamic simulation, both physics-based. As such, the entire computation must be repeated when the keyhole geometry changes. In this study, a data-based deep-learning model for predicting laser-beam absorptance in full-penetration laser keyhole welding is proposed. The model uses a set of keyhole top- and bottom-aperture as inputs. From these, an artificial intelligence (AI) model is trained to predict the laser-energy absorptance value. For the training dataset, various keyhole geometries (i.e., top- and bottom-aperture shapes) are hypothetically created, upon which the ray-tracing model is employed to compute the corresponding absorptance values. An image classification model, ResNet, is employed as a learning recognizer of features to predict absorptance. For image regression, several modifications are applied to the structure. Five model depths are tested, and the optimal AI architecture is used to predict the absorptance with an R2 accuracy of 99.76% within 1.66 s for 740 keyhole shapes. Using this model, several keyhole parameters affecting the keyhole absorptance are identified.

Abstract:
Keyhole laser welding is the benchmark for deep-penetration joining processes. It needs high incident laser beam power densities at the workpiece surface to take place. The gaseous phase plays a fundamental role to keep the deep and narrow keyhole cavity open during the process. The plasma created in this process is a mixture of ionized metal vapors and the environmental gas and it develops inside the keyhole (keyhole plasma) and above the workpiece surface (plasma plume). The presence of plasma implicates absorption, scattering, and refraction of laser beam rays. These phenomena alter the power density of the laser beam irradiating the workpiece surface and thus affect the resulting welding process. In this work, a mathematical and numerical model has been developed to calculate the keyhole shape taking into account the plasma absorption effects. The model considers the keyhole walls as the liquid-vapor interface and computes the keyhole geometry applying a local energy balance at this interface. In addition, the model takes into account the multiple reflections effects inside the cavity through an iterative ray-tracing technique, and calculates the absorption mechanism due to inverse Bremsstrahlung for each ray along its segmented path inside the keyhole. Results show the effect of plasma properties on the keyhole shape and depth.

    title = "The calculation of keyhole depth based on the primary absorption of front keyhole wall in laser deep-penetration welding",

Abstract:
The establishment of an accurate prediction model of keyhole depth during laser welding is of great significance for predicting the weld depth or pre-selecting suitable welding process parameters. In this paper, based on the primary absorption of the incident laser by the front keyhole wall, the tilt angle of the keyhole wall was calculated point by point according to the equilibrium relationship between the laser energy absorbed by the material and the energy required for evaporation at any position of the front keyhole wall. A prediction model for the keyhole depth in laser deep penetration welding has been established by taking into account the laser optical parameters, the focusing system parameters, the welding process parameters, and the material properties. The transformation law of the front keyhole wall profile, the Fresnel absorption coefficient, and the keyhole depth with laser power, welding speed, focusing focal length, and other parameters was calculated in the model, which is basically in line with the consensus. At the same time, the keyhole depth results of calculations and measurements under some parameter conditions were compared. It can be found that the prediction model of keyhole depth during laser deep penetration welding can be used to approximate the calculation of weld depth, and the feasibility of the model was preliminarily verified. Moreover, combined with previous experimental results, the conclusion that the primary absorption of front keyhole wall is the key factor determining the keyhole depth can be re-verified by using mathematical calculations. It also shows that the complex energy coupling law in keyhole has a noticeable difference in the influence of different physical phenomena during laser deep penetration welding.

## pqac-00000000

From text 'kaplan1994amodelof pages 9-11'.

A. Kaplan. A model of deep penetration laser welding based on calculation of the keyhole profile. Journal of Physics D, 27:1805-1814, Sep 1994. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3727/27/9/002, doi:10.1088/0022-3727/27/9/002. This article has 587 citations.

The excerpt describes Kaplan’s model as a point-by-point, vertically discretized calculation of the keyhole energy balance. The keyhole-wall position is obtained by balancing laser energy coupled into the workpiece against heat-conduction losses and optical/plasma losses. Heat conduction is represented using moving line heat sources located near the front wall, whose superposed temperature fields determine the melt-pool profile. The gaseous state inside the keyhole is calculated to obtain plasma parameters and inverse-Bremsstrahlung absorption. The model includes direct Fresnel absorption, absorption after multiple reflections, plasma-plume absorption, and beam power striking the workpiece outside the keyhole. The excerpt reports that direct Fresnel absorption and multiple-reflection absorption dominate, while plasma absorption is negligible; the latter is also supported by the observed polarization dependence of penetration depth. Increasing welding speed reduces the number of reflections and overall absorption, while the keyhole opening angle increases as penetration decreases. A plume absorption coefficient of 100 m⁻¹ gives approximately 8% plume loss. The supplied pages do not contain the explicit moving-line-source, Fresnel-absorption, or local-wall-inclination formulas, nor the numerical comparison between calculated and measured keyhole depths.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'kaplan1994amodelof pages 1-3'.

A. Kaplan. A model of deep penetration laser welding based on calculation of the keyhole profile. Journal of Physics D, 27:1805-1814, Sep 1994. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3727/27/9/002, doi:10.1088/0022-3727/27/9/002. This article has 587 citations.

The excerpt describes Kaplan’s model as a point-by-point calculation of the keyhole wall. Its central governing condition is a local energy balance: laser power absorbed at the wall—through Fresnel absorption, multiple internal reflections, and plasma absorption—must balance heat-conduction losses (and, in the stated introduction, convection-related losses). Heat conduction is obtained from a moving line-source/Rosenthal temperature field and Fourier’s law; the excerpt shows the radial simplification as q = −λ∇T, with the displayed form involving the radial temperature derivative, but it does not provide the complete moving-line-source equation. The local balance determines the wall inclination, while a separate pressure balance is required to keep the keyhole open; metal-vapour pressure counters surface tension. The model abandons rotational symmetry and computes front and back walls separately, producing an asymmetric profile because upstream/front-wall conduction losses differ from those at the rear. It includes metal-vapour thermodynamics, flow, plasma damping above the workpiece, and mean plasma absorption in the keyhole. The supplied pages do not contain the explicit Fresnel-absorption formula, the full wall-angle equation, or comparisons between predicted and measured keyhole depths, so those details cannot be recovered from this excerpt.

## pqac-00000002

From text 'kaplan1994amodelof pages 6-7'.

A. Kaplan. A model of deep penetration laser welding based on calculation of the keyhole profile. Journal of Physics D, 27:1805-1814, Sep 1994. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3727/27/9/002, doi:10.1088/0022-3727/27/9/002. This article has 587 citations.

The excerpt describes Kaplan’s keyhole model as a coupled thermal, optical, gaseous-phase, and hydrodynamic calculation. After determining the keyhole profile, the vapor state is calculated element by element using local thermodynamic equilibrium and Saha’s equation for ionization. Plasma heat transfer is treated as non-radiative, with inverse Bremsstrahlung as the dominant CO2-laser absorption mechanism. Multiple reflections are represented through a reflection coefficient that varies with wall angle; rays are partially absorbed while crossing the plasma, and the mean ray path in a blind keyhole is taken as 1.5 times the keyhole depth. A constant mean plasma absorption coefficient of approximately 100 m^-1 is reported as adequate, with Beer–Lambert attenuation used for transmitted or absorbed intensity. Plasma heat conduction is modeled as radial conduction toward the keyhole wall, with absorbed plasma power distributed uniformly over the element volume. The excerpt also indicates cylindrical heat conduction solved using boundary conditions at the axis and wall, and hydrodynamics obtained from momentum and mass balances, including Hagen–Poiseuille friction, surface-tension pressure, evaporation, and Knudsen-layer effects. Figure 4 compares predicted welding depth against measured depth versus welding speed for 4 and 10 kW, but the excerpt does not provide numerical comparison values. The requested moving-line-source formula, explicit Fresnel formula, and local-wall-inclination equation are not fully visible here.

## pqac-00000003

From text 'kaplan1994amodelof pages 3-5'.

A. Kaplan. A model of deep penetration laser welding based on calculation of the keyhole profile. Journal of Physics D, 27:1805-1814, Sep 1994. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3727/27/9/002, doi:10.1088/0022-3727/27/9/002. This article has 587 citations.

Kaplan’s model determines the keyhole profile by applying a local energy balance at each wall point. The absorbed laser power is balanced against heat losses into the workpiece by conduction and convection. Heat conduction is obtained from Rosenthal’s moving line-source temperature field, expressed using modified Bessel functions K0 and K1; the source has power per unit depth P′ and produces a temperature singularity at its location. The relevant transport parameter is the modified Péclet number Pe′ = U_w/K. The wall is constrained to the evaporation temperature, allowing the source strength and local heat flow to be evaluated point-by-point. The laser intensity is modeled as a Gaussian-like distribution determined by laser power, focusing number, wavelength, and beam-quality factor, with the focal radius and Rayleigh length controlling its depth variation. Fresnel absorption supplies the locally absorbed power in the simplest calculation, while plasma absorption and multiple-reflection effects are added in a second calculation. The local wall inclination is obtained by geometrically transforming the absorbed intensity so that it equals the conductive and convective heat loss. Front and rear walls differ because of the upstreaming effect associated with welding speed. The excerpt describes the iterative profile construction but does not provide the complete displayed formulas for Fresnel absorption, wall angle, or comparisons with measured keyhole depths.

This excerpt describes Kaplan’s treatment of absorption in the keyhole model rather than presenting the complete governing equations. The calculation is performed in two runs: the first uses only direct Fresnel absorption to obtain a preliminary keyhole profile and gaseous state; the second includes additional absorption mechanisms. The incident beam is attenuated by plasma absorption in the plume, first-pass plasma absorption, Fresnel absorption at the wall, and multiple reflections. Plasma attenuation follows Beer–Lambert behavior, with plume absorption expressed as η_pl = 1 − exp(−α_IB h_pl), while first-pass plasma absorption is represented by η_IB,1 = 1 − exp(−α_IB l). The reflected intensity after n reflections is represented using the Fresnel reflection coefficient, and a mean reflection number is estimated geometrically from the keyhole wall angle. The energy balance uses the local beam intensity multiplied by the local Fresnel absorption coefficient; the beam intensity already includes plasma attenuation. Outside the keyhole, near-normal incidence produces weak absorption, and a critical angle of π/2 identifies the keyhole start. The excerpt does not provide the moving-line-source heat-conduction formula, the explicit local-wall-inclination equation, or comparisons between calculated and measured keyhole depths.

It does, however, describe a related dynamical keyhole-front model and provides equations that may be useful for comparison. The model assumes a stationary keyhole front whose normal displacement is zero: the welding-speed component normal to the wall balances the laser-driven drilling velocity, giving Vd = Vw cos α. Using a piston-model approximation, the drilling velocity is assumed proportional to locally absorbed laser intensity, Vd = k Iabs = k I0 A(α) sin α. The local absorptivity is represented by a Fresnel-like relation, A(α) = A0(sin α)^q, with q approximately 0.1. Under low welding speed and small q, the keyhole-front inclination scales as α ≈ Vw/(kI0A0). The excerpt also reports that, above a critical welding speed, penetration depth scales inversely with welding speed, e ∝ 1/Vw; larger focal spots extend the range where this scaling applies. These results concern Fabbro’s model rather than Kaplan’s specific formulation, so the requested energy balance, moving-line-source expression, and measured-depth comparison are absent here.

The excerpt describes Kaplan’s model qualitatively but does not reproduce the governing equations, explicit energy-balance formula, moving-line-source heat-conduction expression, Fresnel absorption equation, local wall-inclination relation, or a numerical comparison with measured keyhole depths. The calculation proceeds by selecting discrete vertical intervals through the workpiece, calculating the gaseous state inside the keyhole, and modeling several absorption mechanisms. Heat conduction losses are based on a moving line-source model. The predicted profile is controlled primarily by direct Fresnel absorption: the front wall intercepts most of the beam and inclines sufficiently to balance its larger upstream convective heat losses, while the rear wall is steeper and receives lower-intensity beam regions. Multiple reflections contribute significantly to total absorption, with their number governed by the mean keyhole-wall angle; plasma absorption is comparatively weak, with plume damping of roughly 10% and a mean plasma absorption coefficient of about 100 m⁻¹ for iron. As welding speed increases, penetration depth decreases, wall angle increases, multiple reflections decrease, and overall absorption falls. The passage does not state how calculated depths compare quantitatively with measurements.

## pqac-00000010

From text 'lankalapalli1996amodelfor pages 9-11'.

Kishore N Lankalapalli, Jay F Tu, and Mark Gartner. A model for estimating penetration depth of laser welding processes. Journal of Physics D, 29:1831-1841, Jul 1996. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3727/29/7/018, doi:10.1088/0022-3727/29/7/018. This article has 199 citations.

The excerpt describes the Lankalapalli–Tu–Gartner model as a conduction-based penetration-depth model in which the heat dissipated from the keyhole is equated to the total incident laser power. The governing temperature field is obtained for a moving line source in a semi-infinite medium using the method of images; equations (20) and (21) express temperature as an integral over the source depth, with real and image-source distances R− and R+. The keyhole is assumed to have a conical shape determined by the evaporation isotherm, although the formulation is not fundamentally restricted to a cone. The model uses thermal diffusivity α and conductivity k as effective fitting parameters representing high-temperature material behavior, rather than necessarily their true liquid-metal values. For validation, a 1010 steel plate fitted to a 1035 steel hub was welded with a 5 kW CO2 laser over 25 power–speed combinations. Width and penetration depth were measured from polished cross-sections. Parameters were fitted using 3.5 and 4.5 kW data, giving α = 0.08 cm² s⁻¹ and k = 0.765 W cm⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Predictions for 3, 4, and 5 kW followed the measured trend: penetration increased with power and decreased with speed. Discrepancies were attributed mainly to uncertain absorbed incident power and departures from assumed keyhole geometry.


---

## pqac-00000011

From text 'lankalapalli1996amodelfor pages 5-7'.

Kishore N Lankalapalli, Jay F Tu, and Mark Gartner. A model for estimating penetration depth of laser welding processes. Journal of Physics D, 29:1831-1841, Jul 1996. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3727/29/7/018, doi:10.1088/0022-3727/29/7/018. This article has 199 citations.

The excerpt describes the analytical basis of the Lankalapalli–Tu–Gartner conical-keyhole model. The weld is treated as a stack of infinitesimally thin layers, each represented by a cylindrical heat source of radius a that moves at constant welding speed ν through an initially uniform, infinite medium. Thermal properties are constant, the cylindrical surface is held at the vaporization temperature TV, and the surrounding temperature approaches the initial temperature T0 far from the source. Axial heat conduction is neglected (Qz ≪ Qr), so heat flow is modeled only in the x–y plane using the quasi-steady advection–diffusion equation ∂²T/∂x² + ∂²T/∂y² − (ν/α)∂T/∂x = 0. The layer solution is expressed with modified Bessel functions and depends primarily on the Péclet number Pe = νa/(2α). The keyhole is assumed conical because its radius, and therefore Pe, varies linearly with depth: Pe(z) = Pe0(1 − z/d̂), reaching zero at the modeled penetration depth d̂. The absorbed power per unit depth is obtained from the radial conductive heat flux at the keyhole wall, Pt = k(TV−T0)g(Pe), with g represented by a polynomial fit. The energy balance equates incident laser power to the integrated absorbed power, Pi = ∫₀^{d̂} Pt(z) dz. This excerpt does not include the model’s comparison with measured penetration depths or its validation results.

## pqac-00000012

From text 'lankalapalli1996amodelfor pages 3-5'.

Kishore N Lankalapalli, Jay F Tu, and Mark Gartner. A model for estimating penetration depth of laser welding processes. Journal of Physics D, 29:1831-1841, Jul 1996. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3727/29/7/018, doi:10.1088/0022-3727/29/7/018. This article has 199 citations.

The excerpt describes a quasi-steady-state model for deep-penetration continuous-wave CO2 laser welding. Its main assumptions are a conical keyhole, complete absorption of laser power at the keyhole, a keyhole wall held at the material vaporization temperature, and equality between actual penetration depth and keyhole depth for high-aspect-ratio welds. The conical geometry is defined by top radius a0 and depth d, with radius decreasing linearly as a(z) = a0(1 − z/d). Because axial conduction is assumed much smaller than radial conduction (Qz << Qr), the keyhole is treated as a sequence of thin cylindrical layers. A 2D cylindrical surface heat-source/conduction model is used in layer 1, while absorbed power per unit depth is converted into an equivalent varying-strength line source for a 3D moving heat-source model in layer 2. The excerpt does not provide the explicit energy-balance equation or the complete closed-form temperature equations; it only identifies the Péclet number Pe = νa/(2α) and the modeling strategy. It states that the model relates penetration depth to incident power, welding speed, and measured weld width, and that validation using experimental data is presented later, but no measured-depth comparisons or numerical validation results appear in this excerpt.

## pqac-00000013

From text 'lankalapalli1996amodelfor pages 11-12'.

Kishore N Lankalapalli, Jay F Tu, and Mark Gartner. A model for estimating penetration depth of laser welding processes. Journal of Physics D, 29:1831-1841, Jul 1996. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3727/29/7/018, doi:10.1088/0022-3727/29/7/018. This article has 199 citations.

The excerpt provides the principal assumptions and qualitative validation of the Lankalapalli–Tu–Gartner (1996) model, but not the full governing or energy-balance equations. The model represents the keyhole as a moving conical surface held at the material vaporization temperature. Heat conduction in the welding direction (z) is assumed negligible relative to conduction in the transverse x and y directions. Molten-pool fluid dynamics are treated as insignificant, and latent heat associated with melting and evaporation is neglected based on earlier findings that these effects are small. The reported validation found a weld profile consistent with the conical-keyhole assumption; however, depth predictions become inaccurate when the actual keyhole departs substantially from a cone. The authors state that the mathematical procedure can be applied to other assumed keyhole geometries, so the model is not intrinsically restricted to a cone. Because laser welding involves complex temperature-dependent thermophysical and phase-change behavior, exact agreement with experiments is not expected. Model parameters therefore need calibration using experimental results from the specific welding process, after which the polynomial relationships and tuned model can be useful for process monitoring. The excerpt does not include the explicit energy balance, heat-conduction solution, or numerical comparison table of predicted versus measured penetration depths.

## pqac-00000014

From text 'lankalapalli1996amodelfor pages 1-3'.

Kishore N Lankalapalli, Jay F Tu, and Mark Gartner. A model for estimating penetration depth of laser welding processes. Journal of Physics D, 29:1831-1841, Jul 1996. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3727/29/7/018, doi:10.1088/0022-3727/29/7/018. This article has 199 citations.

The excerpt provides only a high-level description of the Lankalapalli, Tu, and Gartner (1996) model; it does not include the detailed governing equations, explicit energy-balance equation, mathematical conical-keyhole geometry, heat-conduction boundary conditions, or numerical comparisons between predicted and measured penetration depths. The model is described as a two-dimensional heat-conduction model combined with a conical keyhole assumption. Penetration depth is related to incident laser power and the Péclet number, with the Péclet number depending on welding speed, keyhole radius, and thermal diffusivity. The model estimates the Péclet number indirectly from weld width measured on the top surface, supporting a potentially non-destructive, model-based, on-line monitoring approach. The modeling framework focuses on the quasi-steady state after a stable keyhole has formed; the excerpt explains that laser-power ramp-up and ramp-down correspond to transient keyhole formation and collapse, while most theoretical models assume a stable keyhole. Validation used welds joining a low-carbon steel hub and plate assembly, produced with a 5 kW CO2 laser over different combinations of laser power and welding speed. The reported outcome is qualitative: predictions were consistent with experimental data and computationally efficient. The pages supplied do not provide the requested equations or detailed measured-versus-predicted penetration-depth results.

## pqac-00000015

From text 'kaplan1994amodelof pages 3-5'.

A. Kaplan. A model of deep penetration laser welding based on calculation of the keyhole profile. Journal of Physics D, 27:1805-1814, Sep 1994. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3727/27/9/002, doi:10.1088/0022-3727/27/9/002. This article has 587 citations.

The excerpt provides partial governing principles for Kaplan’s 1994 keyhole model, which may be relevant background for the Lankalapalli–Tu–Gartner 1996 conical-keyhole model, but it does not explicitly identify that 1996 model or report its validation against measured penetration depths. The model treats the keyhole wall through a local energy balance: absorbed laser intensity is equated to heat losses from the wall, primarily conduction into the workpiece and convection-related effects. Heat conduction is calculated using Rosenthal’s moving line-source temperature field, expressed with modified Bessel functions and a modified Peclet number Pe_l = U_w/κ. The wall reaches the evaporation temperature, which determines the source strength and local heat flow. Front and rear walls are treated separately because the moving heat source creates asymmetric heat flow; the front wall experiences greater losses than the rear wall. The wall inclination is obtained geometrically from the local balance, and the profile is integrated point-by-point from the top surface downward until the front and rear walls intersect. Laser input is represented by a Gaussian-like intensity distribution, with beam parameters determined by laser power, focusing optics, wavelength, and beam quality. The calculation is performed first with direct Fresnel absorption and then repeated with additional absorption mechanisms. No explicit conical-shape equation, measured-depth comparison, or validation results appear in this excerpt.

## pqac-00000016

From text 'fabbro2010physicalmechanismscontrolling pages 4-7'.

R. Fabbro. Physical mechanisms controlling keyhole and melt pool dynamics during laser welding. ArXiv, pages 211-241, Jan 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.1533/9781845699819.3.211, doi:10.1533/9781845699819.3.211. This article has 12 citations.

Fabbro’s front-wall drilling model treats the keyhole as a piston-like process: laser energy produces evaporation pressure at the front wall, while material is removed mainly through lateral melt ejection. Under stationary conditions, the drilling velocity Vd is proportional to absorbed intensity, Vd = k Iabs, with k approximately 3 × 10^-11 m^3 J^-1 for the stated regime. For welding, the inclined front wall is stationary in the laser-beam frame when the welding-speed component normal to the wall equals the drilling velocity: Vw cos(a) = Vd. The absorbed intensity is modeled as Iabs = I0 A(a) sin(a), and the simplifying assumption A(a) = A0 gives tan(a) = Vw/(k I0 A0). Assuming a uniform incident intensity over a circular spot of diameter D, high and approximately constant absorptivity, and negligible multiple reflections, the penetration depth is L = k I0 A0 D/Vw = (4 A0 k/π) P/(D Vw). Thus depth scales linearly with laser power P, inversely with spot diameter D, and inversely with welding speed Vw. At low speed, the model predicts Iabs = Vw/k, a self-regulating absorbed intensity independent of incident intensity. The excerpt reports that the P/D and 1/Vw scaling laws were experimentally observed in Nd:YAG laser welding; it provides no LPBF depth comparison.


---

## pqac-00000017

From text 'fabbro2010meltpooland pages 6-9'.

R. Fabbro. Melt pool and keyhole behaviour analysis for deep penetration laser welding. Journal of Physics D: Applied Physics, 43:445501, Nov 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3727/43/44/445501, doi:10.1088/0022-3727/43/44/445501. This article has 452 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Fabbro’s front-wall model treats the keyhole front as being in local stationary equilibrium between the welding-speed-induced motion and laser drilling. The front wall is inclined by angle α to the vertical beam, and the normal component of material motion must equal the normal drilling velocity: Vd = Vw cos α. Using the piston-model assumption, drilling velocity is taken to be proportional to absorbed laser intensity. For a uniform incident beam, Vd = k Iabs = k I0 A(α) sin α, where k is a material- and condition-dependent proportionality factor, I0 is incident intensity, A(α) is angle-dependent absorptivity, and sin α represents the incidence-angle factor. Absorptivity is approximated with a Fresnel-like law, A(α) = A0(sin α)^q, with q approximately 0.1. For small q and low welding speeds, the model predicts α ≈ Vw/(k I0 A0), consistent with measured near-linear increases of front-wall angle with welding speed and similar intensity scaling. The excerpt reports penetration-depth behavior rather than a complete depth equation: above a critical speed Vwc, depth scales as e ∝ 1/Vw; below Vwc, depth increases more slowly and approaches saturation under static conditions. Larger focal spots extend the range where 1/Vw scaling applies. No direct LPBF comparison or numerical comparison with measured LPBF depths is provided; the experimental comparisons described concern laser welding, including stainless and mild steel.


---

## pqac-00000018

From text 'fabbro2020depthdependenceand pages 3-5'.

Remy Fabbro. Depth dependence and keyhole stability at threshold, for different laser welding regimes. Applied Sciences, 10:1487, Feb 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/app10041487, doi:10.3390/app10041487. This article has 69 citations.

Fabbro’s model separates low-speed, high-aspect-ratio keyholes from high-speed, low-aspect-ratio regimes. The basic scaling model assumes that absorbed laser power A(R)P is uniformly distributed along the keyhole depth and balances conductive losses, represented through a Peclet-dependent function approximated as g(Pe) ≈ mPe + n. This gives R = R0/(1 + Vw/V0), so keyhole depth decreases approximately inversely with welding speed at high speeds and saturates as speed decreases. Equivalently, A(R)P/(dR) = a + b(Vwd), with a and b determined by thermal properties and the conductive-loss approximation. The threshold incident power for R = 1 follows from this scaling and provides a normalized relation R = A(R)P/[A(1)Pt]. At high welding speeds, the keyhole front is modeled as an inclined surface rather than a vertical cylinder, with R = 1/tan(α). The generalized piston model treats the front as stationary in the laser-beam frame: its motion combines welding velocity Vw and a recoil-pressure-driven drilling velocity Vd normal to the surface. Stationarity requires Vd = Vw cos(α). For R below roughly 3, the direct beam dominates depth formation and later reflected-beam contributions are neglected. The excerpt reports validation of the scaling law against macro-welding data for steel and copper, but provides no LPBF-specific depth comparison here.

## pqac-00000019

From text 'fabbro2010meltpooland pages 10-12'.

R. Fabbro. Melt pool and keyhole behaviour analysis for deep penetration laser welding. Journal of Physics D: Applied Physics, 43:445501, Nov 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3727/43/44/445501, doi:10.1088/0022-3727/43/44/445501. This article has 452 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt provides partial information relevant to Fabbro’s front-wall drilling/keyhole model, but it does not reproduce the complete governing equations, the explicit piston-force balance, or the drilling-velocity equation. It states that melt-pool motion is initially driven by side flows beneath the focal spot through a local “piston effect,” while coupling to the keyhole depends on front-wall inclination and the dynamic pressure of the ejected vapor plume. At high welding speeds, the model predicts a penetration-depth dependence scaling approximately with 1/Vw, with focal-spot diameter controlling the extent of that regime. At low welding speeds, the absorbed intensity at the keyhole front is predicted to depend primarily on welding speed rather than incident intensity; reduced evaporation pressure allows keyhole collapse and limits stable penetration. The excerpt gives the resulting maximum stable-depth relation for 304 stainless steel, emax(mm) ≈ 1.5 P(kW), together with the stability condition Vw(m/min)·D(mm) > 1. It also reports that a suitably adjusted argon side jet can stabilize the keyhole, increase penetration by about 40%, and eliminate porosity. No direct comparisons with LPBF measurements are included; the stated experimental context is conventional laser welding.
